HRP catalyses SCN− oxidation through two one-electron transfer steps and is concurrently inactivated due to the formation of CN−, the product of the hydrolysis of thiocyanogen.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

HRP catalyze SCN− oxidation by one-electron transfers, while LPO catalyzes SCN oxidation by two-electron transfers, which is responsible for its much higher catalytic efficiency in SCN− oxidation than that of HRP.
HRP is a poor SCN− oxidizer due to the inactivation by the SCN− oxidation product, CN−, formed in a large amount.
the catalytic turnover of HRP in SCN− oxidation is limited by the inactivation of the active site due to the higher affinity of CN− formed as an intermediate for the active site of HRP.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HRP is inactivated by SCN− and CN− formed in its catalytic turnover.
HRP is a poor catalyst for SCN− oxidation as it is inactivated by SCN− and the product CN−, which is not the case with LPO.
the low catalytic turnover of HRP in SCN− oxidation is due to the formation of CN− from the reaction of thiocyanogen and H2O and the concurrent inactivation of HRP by CN−.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HRP is a better oxidant for SCN− at low concentrations, but LPO is a better oxidizing agent for SCN− at physiological concentrations.
the slow rate of SCN oxidation by HRP is due to its high affinity for CN− and not due to its slow oxidation of SCN−.
the low catalytic turnover of HRP in the oxidation of SCN− is due to the formation of the inactivated HRP-CN− adduct.
